We proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to \infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{1}{2x+1}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}\frac{1}{2x+1}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{[\frac{1}{2}\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡|2x+1|]}_{0}^{a} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x+1|]}_{0}^{a} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }(\operatorname{ln}⁡|2a+1|-\operatorname{ln}⁡|1|) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }(\operatorname{ln}⁡|2a+1|) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot (\infty ) \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the integral is divergent.

First, we substitute $u=2x-3.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2\,⟹\,\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u=\text{d}x.
$$

Since $u\to -\infty $ when $x\to -\infty ,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=2x-3$ is as follows:

| $x$ | $1$ | $-\infty $ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $-1$ | $-\infty $ |

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{1}\frac{1}{(2x-3)^{5}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\infty }^{-1}\frac{1}{{u}^{5}}\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to -\infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{1}\frac{1}{(2x-3)^{5}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\infty }^{-1}\frac{1}{{u}^{5}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\infty }^{-1}{u}^{-5}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{-1}{u}^{-5}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[\frac{{u}^{-4}}{-4}]}_{a}^{-1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{8}\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[\frac{1}{{u}^{4}}]}_{a}^{-1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{8}\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }[1-\frac{1}{{a}^{4}}] \\  & =-\frac{1}{8}\cdot (1-0) \\  & =-\frac{1}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we substitute $u=3t-2.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t}=3\,⟹\,\text{d}u=3\text{d}t.
$$

Since $u\to \infty $ when $t\to \infty ,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=3t-2$ is as follows:

| $t$ | $2$ | $\infty $ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $4$ | $\infty $ |

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

$$
{\int }_{2}^{\infty }\frac{3}{\sqrt{(3t-2)^{5}}}\,\text{d}t={\int }_{4}^{\infty }\frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{5}}}\,\text{d}u
$$

Finally, we proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to \infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{\infty }\frac{3}{\sqrt{(3t-2)^{5}}}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{4}^{\infty }\frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{5}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{4}^{\infty }{u}^{-5/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{4}^{a}{u}^{-5/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[-\frac{2}{3}{u}^{-3/2}]}_{4}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[{u}^{-3/2}]}_{4}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }[\frac{1}{(a)^{3/2}}-\frac{1}{(4)^{3/2}}] \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\cdot (0-\frac{1}{8}) \\  & =\frac{1}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

We proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to \infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{5}{\sqrt[3]{{y}^{8}}}\,\text{d}y & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{1}^{a}\frac{5}{\sqrt[3]{{y}^{8}}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =5{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{1}^{a}{y}^{-8/3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =5{lim}_{a\to \infty }{[-\frac{3}{5}{y}^{-5/3}]}_{1}^{a} \\  & =-3\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[\frac{1}{\sqrt[3]{{y}^{5}}}]}_{1}^{a} \\  & =-3\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }(\frac{1}{\sqrt[3]{{a}^{5}}}-\frac{1}{\sqrt[3]{{1}^{5}}}) \\  & =-3(0-1) \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we substitute $u=2x+1.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2\,⟹\,\text{d}u=2\text{d}x.
$$

Since $u\to -\infty $ when $x\to -\infty ,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=2x+1$ is as follows:

| $x$ | $-\infty $ | $-1$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $-\infty $ | $-1$ |

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{-1}\frac{6}{(2x+1)^{4}}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-\infty }^{-1}\frac{3}{{u}^{4}}\,\text{d}u
$$

Finally, we proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to -\infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{-1}\frac{3}{{u}^{4}}\,\text{d}u & =3{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{-1}{u}^{-4}\,\text{d}u \\  & =3{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[-\frac{1}{3}{u}^{-3}]}_{a}^{-1} \\  & =-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[\frac{1}{{u}^{3}}]}_{a}^{-1} \\  & =-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }[\frac{1}{(-1)^{3}}-\frac{1}{{a}^{3}}] \\  & =-(-1-0) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$
